tip: 'çalmayı' = 'çal' + -ma + -yı: -ma turns a verb into a noun 'playing', then object-marker -yı marks it as the thing being learned.
'ekmeğine': the final k of 'ekmek' softens to ğ before a vowel ending, so 'ekmek' plus its suffixes becomes 'ekmeğine'.
'dolmayı' is the object and 'yaptı' is the verb at the end: Turkish normally puts the verb last, so objects like 'dolmayı' come before it.
'benim' in 'benim adım' is optional because 'adım' already means 'my name'. Add 'benim' only to stress whose name it is.
'bugünkü' = 'bugün' (today) + -kü: the -ki/-kü ending makes 'the one of that time', so 'bugünkü toplantı' = today's meeting.
'uzaklaşmalıyız' = 'uzaklaş' + -malı + -yız: -malı/-meli means 'must' and -yız marks we, so 'we must move away'.
'süredir' = 'süre' (time) + -dir: here -dir means 'for/since', so 'uzun süredir' means 'for a long time now'.
'bahçesi' = 'bahçe' + -si: after a vowel-ending noun, a buffer s carries the -si ending, giving 'its garden'.
'uyuyamadım' = I couldn't sleep: the -yama inside the verb means inability, so it's not 'didn't' but 'couldn't'.
'verelim' = let's give: adding -elim/-alım to a verb stem makes a 'let's do it' suggestion, like 'gidelim' = let's go.
Turkish 'makes decisions' with 'almak' (to take): 'kararlar aldık' means we took, that is made, decisions.
'çıkmış' uses -mış for something inferred rather than watched happen, fitting 'the bread has evidently just come out'.
'rağmen' (despite) makes the word before it take the -a ending: 'olmasına rağmen' = despite it being cold.
'pideci' = 'pide' + -ci: the -ci ending names the person who makes or sells something, so 'pideci' is the pide maker.
Turkish good-wishes often take the plural. 'yolculuklar' is the plural of 'yolculuk' (journey); 'iyi yolculuklar' means have a good trip.
The suffix -ce turns an adjective into a manner adverb. 'güzel' means nice, 'güzelce' means nicely.
The suffix -la/-le means with and builds manner adverbs. 'heyecan' is excitement, 'heyecanla' means excitedly.
A position word like 'karşısında' (across from) needs the owner marked with -ın: 'parkın karşısında' means across from the park.
'güle güle' is said by the person staying to the one leaving. The one departing says 'hoşça kal' or 'hoşça kalın' instead.
'geçmiş olsun' is a fixed get-well phrase, literally may it be past; you say it to anyone sick or in trouble.
For pleased to meet you Turkish uses the past tense: 'memnun oldum' is literally I became pleased.
A final k softens to ğ before a vowel ending. 'sokak' plus the -a ending becomes 'sokağa', meaning to the street.
'kusura bakmayın' is a set apology, literally don't look at the fault, meaning no offense or excuse me.
Past continuous stacks -yor plus -du. 'bekliyor' (is waiting) becomes 'bekliyorduk', we were waiting.
To say need to, use the verb as a noun with a personal ending plus 'lazım'. 'düşünmem lazım' means I need to think.
A verb becomes an object with -ma plus the object marker -yı. 'oynamayı öğretti' means taught the playing, that is, taught how to play.
Adjectives and nouns are negated with the separate word 'değil', not a suffix. 'hazır değilim' means I'm not ready.
The -u/-ı object ending marks a definite object. 'tansiyonumu' (my blood pressure) ends in -u because it's the specific thing measured.
The -ip ending chains verbs that share one final tense. 'buluşup yedik' means met up and ate; only 'yedik' carries the past.
Future tense is -acak/-ecek. 'yaz' (write) plus -acak gives 'yazacak', will write.
